title: Node.js
summary: JavaScript outside the browser: servers, scripts, npm and the event loop.

lessons.title: Node.js: running JavaScript outside the browser

concept.text:
Node.js is a program that runs JavaScript on your computer or a server instead of inside a web page. It adds abilities browsers forbid, such as reading files and listening for network connections.

Node code is organised into **modules** (files that export things) and **packages** (other people's modules, installed with npm).
concept.analogy: JavaScript in a browser is a chef working a food truck: limited tools, strict safety rules. Node.js moves the same chef into a full restaurant kitchen with access to the pantry (files) and the delivery door (network).

steps.title: Run a file
steps.text: Install Node from nodejs.org, save code in a file, and run it from a terminal.

steps.title: Export and import
steps.text: One file exports, another imports. This is the modern ES module syntax.

steps.title: Use npm
steps.text: `npm init -y` creates package.json, the project's manifest. `npm install` adds packages and records them there.

steps.title: Use built-in modules
steps.text: Node ships with modules for files, paths, HTTP and more. Prefix them with `node:`.
steps.code:
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'
const text = await readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8')

challenge.prompt: Write the two files for a tiny project: `temperature.js` exports `toF(c)` and `toC(f)`, and `app.js` imports both and prints 100°C in Fahrenheit and 32°F in Celsius.
challenge.hint: F = C × 9/5 + 32. Use `export const` in one file and `import { toF, toC } from './temperature.js'` in the other.
challenge.solution:
// temperature.js
export const toF = (c) => (c * 9) / 5 + 32
export const toC = (f) => ((f - 32) * 5) / 9

// app.js
import { toF, toC } from './temperature.js'
console.log(toF(100)) // 212
console.log(toC(32))  // 0

takeaways: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser with access to files and the network.
Modules split code across files with export and import.
npm installs packages and package.json records what your project needs.

lessons.title: Node.js: the event loop and a web server

concept.text:
Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, yet it can serve thousands of connections. The trick is the **event loop**: slow work (network, disk) is handed off, and Node keeps running other code. When the slow work finishes, its callback joins a queue and runs when the thread is free.

This is why Node code is full of `async` and `await`, and why you must never block the thread with a long calculation.
concept.analogy: The event loop is one very fast waiter. They take an order, pass it to the kitchen, and immediately serve another table instead of standing at the stove. When a dish is ready, the kitchen rings a bell and the waiter delivers it.

visual.caption: One turn of the event loop.

nodes.label: Run current code
nodes.detail: Until the call stack is empty

steps.title: Predict the order
steps.text: Synchronous code runs first, then promise callbacks (microtasks), then timers, even a timer of 0 ms.

steps.title: Create a server
steps.text: This callback runs once per request. Node is not blocked while waiting for the next one.

steps.title: Use a framework for real apps
steps.text: Express (or Fastify, Hono) adds routing so you can map methods and paths to handlers.
steps.code:
import express from 'express'
const app = express()
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id }))
app.listen(3000)

steps.title: Handle errors
steps.text: Wrap awaited calls in try/catch and return a proper status code such as 500 instead of crashing.

interactive.starter:
// Before you press Run: what order will these print in?
console.log('1. start')

setTimeout(() => console.log('4. timer (0 ms)'), 0)

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3. promise'))

console.log('2. end of script')

challenge.prompt: Write an async function `fetchAll(urls)` that requests every URL **at the same time** and returns the parsed JSON results in order. Test it with two JSONPlaceholder user URLs.
challenge.hint: `Promise.all(array.map(async ...))` starts everything at once and waits for all of them.

takeaways: Node is single-threaded but non-blocking thanks to the event loop.
Order of execution: synchronous code, then promises, then timers and I/O.
Promise.all runs independent async work concurrently.

lessons.title: Node.js mini project: a REST API in memory

concept.text: You will design the core of a REST API for notes: a router that maps a method and path to a handler, backed by an in-memory array. This is exactly what Express does for you, so building a tiny version removes the mystery.
concept.analogy: A router is a hotel switchboard. A call comes in for a room (method + path) and the operator connects it to the right guest (handler function).

steps.title: Store the data
steps.text: An array of note objects stands in for a database.

steps.title: Write handlers
steps.text: Each handler takes the request and returns a status and a body. Unknown ids return 404.

steps.title: Route requests
steps.text: Match the method and path, pull the id out of the path, and call the right handler. In a real server you would wire this function into `createServer`.

challenge.prompt: Add support for `PATCH /notes/:id` that updates a note's text and returns 200 with the updated note. Return 400 if the body has no `text`.
challenge.hint: Add the branch after the note is found. `Object.assign(note, { text: body.text })` updates it in place.

takeaways: A REST API is a router plus handlers plus a data store.
Return accurate status codes: 201 created, 204 deleted, 400 bad input, 404 missing.
Frameworks like Express automate the routing you just wrote by hand.
